paras: The posse hanging on Uvas Creek and threatened lynching at Watsonville took place in January 1882, when a California deputy sheriff's posse hunting the men wanted for the stabbing of Charles Rossi strung up an unnamed man, called a Mexican in one dispatch, to make him reveal where the fugitives were hiding. The posse then captured Ignacio Tejada at a hollow tree, and friends of Rossi at Watsonville threatened to lynch the prisoners before officers sent them to Santa Cruz by train. The hanged man survived and the prisoners were not lynched; Tejada was later sentenced to seven years in San Quentin.

According to a Watsonville dispatch of January 4, uninvited 'toughs' from Whisky Hill fired pistols at Rossi's house, in the redwoods about eight miles from Watsonville, during a wedding party there. When Rossi came out to object, one Jose Tejada was said to have stabbed him in the back, and a brother of Tejada to have shot an Indian teamster. Deputy Sheriff John Gaffey's posse went after them, and the dispatch said that if Tejada were found 'by any other than the Sheriff's party he will be swung up to the most convenient tree.'

Gaffey's posse of John Royce, Tom Ritchie, L. Galindo and Jim Murphy spent five days searching the mountains around Loma Prieta and the cabins on Uvas Creek in Santa Clara County. Told by a 'Californian' that the fugitives were hidden by a man whose house they had already searched, they returned there near 2 a.m. on January 7. When he denied knowing anything, Gaffey's account says, 'they then swung the man up until his tongue protruded,' and raised him again before he agreed to talk if they would not hang him. The Eureka Daily Sentinel's shorter dispatch said he was strung up until 'nearly choked to death.'

He led them to a hut, where another man pointed out a hollow tree only after Royce jumped at him with the rope. Twenty-five to thirty shots were exchanged at the tree; Tejada, wounded in the arm, surrendered, and the man said to have stabbed Rossi was shot and escaped.

At the Watsonville jail Tejada fell into convulsions and said he was afraid of being lynched. With 'friends of Rossi declaring that Judge Lynch should preside over their destinies,' officers took the prisoners out the back of the jail to the Santa Cruz train under guard. A wire of January 10 said a mob had followed the posse through town and 'threatened to lynch the prisoners.'

On January 21 Judge Logan at Santa Cruz sentenced 'Ygnacio Tejada' to seven years in San Quentin for shooting at an Indian named Jesus and for an old jail-break offense. No report of action against the posse for the hanging, or of the fate of Leal, Rossi or Jose Tejada, was found.

The story first ran in Pacific coast dispatches in Nevada and California papers on January 8 and 9. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union, under 'Outlaws Captured in a Hollow Tree—A Desperate Fight,' relayed Gaffey's account of the hanging without comment and said the posse 'deserve great praise' for capturing 'these villains.'

Eastern readers saw a briefer January 10 wire, 'A Fight With Murderers,' in the Daily Republican of Delaware on January 11 and the Millheim Journal on January 19. It called Tejada and Leal 'murderers,' credited 'a posse of police,' and left out the hanging. The Savannah Morning News variant of January 14 identified Tejada as 'the Mexican who shot the Indian, Jesus'; no report gave the episode a racial motive.

The January 7 dispatches said one fugitive escaped wounded; the Savannah version said Leal escaped, shot through the body, after the posse fired the tree; the January 10 wire said both were taken, Leal 'mortally wounded.' That wire placed the fight the evening before January 10 and Savannah credited a 'Deputy Sheriff White,' while the Watsonville dispatches written the day the posse returned name Gaffey and put the fight at 2 a.m. on January 7. The January 4 dispatch named Jose Tejada as the stabber and his brother as the shooter, whereas later reports tie Ignacio Tejada to the shooting of 'Jesus.'

reader.title: Posse hanging on Uvas Creek and threatened lynching at Watsonville
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A deputy sheriff's posse half-hanged an uncharged man to force information from him (A3, A5), and a crowd at Watsonville threatened to lynch the captured prisoners, who were removed by train (A5, A7, A8); no one was killed by either.

The man strung up by the five-man posse survived and told them where the fugitives were (A3, A5), and the Watsonville crowd's threat against the prisoners was not carried out because officers took them to Santa Cruz (A5, A7, A8); no one was killed by a group acting outside the law.

Two differently worded Watsonville dispatches of Jan. 7 agree on the hanging, the hollow-tree fight and the removal to Santa Cruz to avoid lynching (A3, A5), and the Jan. 10 wires independently report the capture and the mob threat (A7, A8), though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Posse leader's account (Gaffey to Sacramento correspondent)
accounts.gist: The posse swung the house owner up twice until he agreed to talk, found the fugitives in a hollow tree, wounded Tejada and the stabber, and took Tejada to Watsonville, from which he was moved as Rossi's friends threatened lynching.

accounts.label: Short Watsonville special
accounts.gist: A Mexican said to have concealed the fugitives was strung up until nearly choked; one fugitive escaped wounded, Tejada surrendered and was sent to Santa Cruz to avoid lynching.

accounts.label: Jan. 10 wire
accounts.gist: Police found Tijada and Leal in a hollow tree; both were taken, Leal mortally wounded; a mob followed and threatened to lynch them.

accounts.label: Savannah variant of Jan. 10 special
accounts.gist: 'Deputy Sheriff White' fired the tree; Tijada was taken, Leal escaped shot through the body; a mob gathered at Watsonville and Tijada was removed to Santa Cruz.

framing.detail: The Sacramento dispatch, headed 'Outlaws Captured in a Hollow Tree—A Desperate Fight,' reported the hanging as Gaffey told it and said the posse 'deserve great praise' for capturing 'these villains.'
The Eureka 'Pacific Coast Advices' item reported the stringing-up flatly among other coast news.
Eastern papers ran the Jan. 10 wire as 'A Fight With Murderers,' calling the fugitives 'murderers' and omitting the hanging.
The Savannah Morning News ran 'A DESPERATE FIGHT,' identifying Tijada as 'the Mexican who shot the Indian, Jesus.'

record_check.dossier: Leal and Tejada were the fugitives the posse hunted; the man strung up was an unnamed house owner said to have hidden them. Tejada (and other prisoners) were the objects of the Watsonville lynching threat.
The hanged man is called 'a certain Mexican' (A3); Tejada is 'the Mexican' (A7). No Black person appears in any report.
